newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria risks delay to much-needed IMF funding.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria risks delay to much-needed IMF funding.

text.p: Urgently needed funding for Bulgaria is likely to be delayed because the country has yet to meet structural reform targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, officals said on Tuesday.
"It is unlikely that the first programme review will be concluded in September as originaly hoped," IMF Sofia representative Franek Rozwadowski told Reuters.

"There has been a considerable progress in implementing structural reforms but some delays have been experienced, particularly in the area of liquidation or rapid privatisation of state owned enterprises," he added.
Under the IMF agreement, which unblocked crucial funding to help Bulgaria meet its foreign debt commitments, Bulgaria stands to gain some $580 million over the next 18 months.
But if the reform delays persist, there is still a real risk of default on payments on Bulgaria's foreign debt of around $9.5 billion, international market sources said.

Bulgaria received the first $115 million tranche in July after sealing a tough reform programme which includes closing scores of loss-making state firms and several insolvent banks, maintaining a tight monetary policy and curbing inflation.
The second $115 million tranche, which was due to be disbursed in September, will be postponed until the government closes down all loss-makers.
"We will stand ready to move ahead rapidly with the review as soon as these structural measures are implemented providing that a sound macroeconomic framework is in place," said Rozwadowski.

The socialist government, in power since January 1995, pledged to close 68 lossmaking state firms and isolate from credits a further 70 problem enterprises like huge metalworks, mines, the National Electricity Company and the State Railways.
But lack of experience in bankruptcy procedures among local authorities and courts has helped to hold up the reforms.

"Bankrupting state firms is a completely new experience in this country. Enterprise managers, the courts and even local government oficials were cought unprepared," Industry Minister Lyubomir Dachev told Reuters.

He said only 14 of the firms earmarked for closed had so far been shut down. Regional courts, bowing to pressure from the firms' management or local authorities, had postponed nine other closures. "The courts are exceeding their powers," Dachev said.

Industrial firms' losses have been reduced to 2.2 billion levs ($10.68 million) in the second half of this year from 7.6 billion levs in 1995 and debts have been cut to 13 billion levs from 18.9 billion levs last year, said Dachev.
Under legislation passed by parliament last month, the 70 problem state companies must present plans to the finance ministry for settling their debts with creditors by year-end.
Bulgaria's industry is in a vicious circle, said Dachev.

Most of the remaining 1,300 enterprises need short-term loans to fulfil existing contracts for their products, but most of the country's cash-strapped banks are reluctant to extend credits, with the exception of few state-owned banks, he said.
Overshooting of Bulgaria's already revised macro-economic targets seems inevitable.
Under a budget revision passed two months ago, annual inflation is assumed to be at 104 percent. But local economists now expect annual inflation of around 150 percent.
